column1: # The settings a user can change, one per line, its fields separated by tabs:
# name (its environment variable), kind (seconds, count:<least>, share, flag,
# choice:<a,b,c>, word, mutators, command, address), default (empty when it is
# worked out), who may set it (project: a project's .sheriff.properties too;
# project:<image>: a project's file too, but only to that image, a tag or a
# digest of it; user: only the user's own file), its name on the settings
# page, and what it does, as sheriff_config and the user's file say. A line
# "## Title" starts a section, which the settings page lists the settings

column6: What happens when a newer build of Sheriff's image is published. always: the server downloads it in the background when it starts and uses it once it is there, so the newest rules apply. check: it only says that a newer one exists, once a session, and keeps using the one you have. never: it does not even ask Docker Hub, for working offline.

The rule profile the code is checked against, such as JAVA, JAVA_HEXAGONAL or TYPESCRIPT, over what the project declares; it applies only to the components written in that profile's language. Empty, the usual choice: the profile the project declares, or else the one its sources call for.

How long one Sheriff analysis may run before it is stopped. Raise it when big components stop on the time limit (900 is the default through WSL's Docker); lower it to learn sooner that an analysis hangs.

How many rounds of Sheriff's own automatic fixers a repair runs, each checked by a new analysis. Empty: rounds go on while each one repairs something, which always ends. A number makes repairs quicker but can leave more errors to fix by hand.

Whether the hooks stop Sheriff at the first error. On: each check is quicker, but the assistant sees one error at a time. Off: every error is found and shown at once. Repairs always look for all of them.

How long the hooks trust a result Sheriff already gave for files that have not changed, before analyzing them again. Higher: fewer analyses and quicker edits. Lower: fresher results, with more analyses.

column5: Times a turn is sent back
column6: How many times in a row the hook at the end of a turn sends the assistant back to work while errors remain, before it lets the turn end anyway. Higher: the assistant insists longer on finishing the work. Lower: you get control back sooner, possibly with errors left.

How many times in a row that hook still sends the assistant back when nothing changed since the last time. 0 lets the turn end at the first stop with no change, which a false positive of the checker that nothing can fix needs; higher values insist more.

Prototype mode, for trying an idea out. On: a component counts as done once Sheriff finds no errors; no tests are asked for, run or measured, by the tools, the hooks or the repair loop. Off: tests and their coverage are required too. Turn it off before the work is kept.

column5: Require green tests to end a turn
column6: Whether a turn may end only with the project's tests passing. On: the hook at the end of a turn runs the tests and measures how well they test what the turn changed, so a turn takes longer to end. Off: that hook checks only the standards.

column5: Test time limit for the tools
column6: How long the project's tests may run when the tools run them (sheriff_fix with verify) before they are stopped. Raise it for a slow test suite.

column5: Test time limit for the hooks and the loop
column6: How long the project's tests may run in the hooks and in the repair loop (sheriff_autofix) before they are stopped. Raise it for a slow test suite.

The share of the lines a change wrote that its tests must run (JaCoCo). Lower it to accept tests that leave some of those lines unrun. A pom.xml's sheriff.coverage, or coverage in a project's .sheriff.properties, wins over this.

The share of the branches of the conditions a change wrote that its tests must take: both ways of every if. Lower it to accept tests that try only some outcomes. A pom.xml's sheriff.branches, or branches in a project's .sheriff.properties, wins over this.

The share of PIT's mutants of the lines a change wrote that its tests must kill: small changes to the code that a good test notices and fails on. Higher asks for stronger tests; lower accepts tests that miss more. A pom.xml's sheriff.mutation, or mutation in a project's .sheriff.properties, wins over this.

Which kinds of mutants PIT makes: mutators or groups (DEFAULTS, STRONGER, ALL), separated by commas. More mutators ask for stronger tests and take longer; ALL makes many mutants that no test can kill. A pom.xml's sheriff.mutators, or mutators in a project's .sheriff.properties, wins over this.
How long the tests may run while their coverage is measured, before the measure is stopped.
How long PIT may run while it tries the mutants, before it is stopped. Mutation testing is the slowest measure: raise it for big changes.

How many passes the repair loop (sheriff_autofix) makes at most, each giving a model a batch of files to fix. Empty: sized from the errors, and grown while they drop. A number caps what one run can cost.
How many files the repair loop gives a model in one pass. Fewer: more focused answers, but more passes. More: fewer passes, but longer prompts, which a model can handle worse.
How many of the profile's rules go into each prompt of the repair loop. Fewer: shorter and cheaper prompts, but the model knows less of the rules the code must meet. Empty: the loop's own limit.

column5: Work on a branch of its own
column6: Whether the repair loop works through git. On: it works on a branch of its own, commits each pass, and stops when a model edits a file outside its batch. Off: it edits your working tree directly, with no branch, commits or check.

Who fixes the code in the repair loop. claude_cli, codex_cli and antigravity_cli use Claude Code, Codex or Antigravity with your login, with no key. anthropic_api and openai_api call those APIs, billed, with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY. local uses a model served on your machine, such as Ollama.

column5: Claude Code time limit per pass
column6: How long one pass of Claude Code may take in the repair loop before it is stopped (AI_BACKEND=claude_cli).
The command the repair loop runs Codex with, without the prompt (AI_BACKEND=codex_cli). Add --model to choose its model.
How long one pass of Codex may take in the repair loop before it is stopped (AI_BACKEND=codex_cli).

The command the repair loop runs Antigravity with, without the prompt (AI_BACKEND=antigravity_cli). Add --model and a name agy models lists to choose its model, such as --model claude-sonnet-5-5-high.
How long one pass of Antigravity may take in the repair loop before it is stopped (AI_BACKEND=antigravity_cli).
The Claude model anthropic_api asks. Its key is read only from the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY variable, never from a file.
Where anthropic_api sends its requests, for a proxy or a gateway. Empty: Anthropic's own API.
The most tokens one answer of anthropic_api may take. Too few cut a file off while it is being written; more cost more only when an answer needs them.
How many times one pass of anthropic_api may read or write a file before it is cut. Higher lets a model do more in one pass, and spend more.
The model openai_api or local asks. Empty: gpt-4o-mini for openai_api, qwen2.5-coder for local. The key is read only from the OPENAI_API_KEY variable, never from a file.
Where openai_api or local sends its requests, such as an LM Studio or vLLM server. Empty: https://api.openai.com/v1 for openai_api, Ollama's http://localhost:11434/v1 for local.
The most tokens one answer of openai_api or local may take. A model that thinks before it answers needs more; too few cut a file off while it is being written.
How many times one pass of openai_api or local may read or write a file before it is cut. Higher lets a model do more in one pass, and spend more.
